But there's a lot we don't know about how those highways actually work, particularly how they give the particles that form the fast solar wind an extra "kick" that sends them zooming at hundreds of kilometers per second.

items.title: New ligand design balances radical generation and catalyst regeneration for challenging chemical reactions
items.desc: Radicals, atoms or molecules that readily react with other substances to form new bonds, are useful tools for building complex substances such as pharmaceuticals. But even when a radical is generated efficiently, the reaction cannot continue unless the catalyst returns to its original state.

items.title: Low-cost sensor tracks soil pH continuously for months across varied soils
items.desc: At first glance, a farm field doesn't seem all that complicated. It's just dirt and crops.

items.title: Tiny wild cat newly identified as a species draws curious visitors in Bolivia
items.desc: A tiny wild cat hidden away in the cloud forests of Bolivia has become an unlikely tourist attraction, drawing a stream of visitors hoping for a glimpse of the animal that scientists have identified as a brand new species.

items.title: A newly discovered mechanism helps cells prevent errors during DNA replication
items.desc: At the scale of individual cells, the human body is constantly in motion. Every second, millions of cells divide, particularly in tissues such as the bone marrow, intestine and skin; neurons and heart muscle cells divide far less frequently. All of this depends on the molecular machinery responsible for copying the billions of chemical units that make up DNA inside the nucleus.

items.title: STEM activities with family and educators expose students to diverse career paths
items.desc: Activities children take part in with family and friends can help shape the fields of study and careers they pursue as adults. A new study published in the International Journal of STEM Education by FIU education researchers Chris Irwin and Zahra Hazari found that STEM activities and conversations with family, friends and teachers are among the strongest factors influencing students' motivations for pursuing STEM (science, technology, engineering and math) careers.

items.title: Antarctica's lost mountains may have helped early life flourish
items.desc: Beneath the vast frozen wastes of Antarctica lie the remains of ancient mountains that have long since eroded. Even though they're no longer standing, they can still reveal a few lost secrets. New research published in Earth and Planetary Science Letters suggests that these vanished peaks may have played a fundamental role in the evolution of complex life on this planet.

items.title: How employers can make good decisions about remote work before the next crisis strikes
items.desc: More than six years after the COVID-19 pandemic began, more than 1 in 5 U.S. workers who can work remotely do so either full time or at least one day a week.

items.title: Lemur uses opera singer's trick to belt out forest songs
items.desc: We are often left open-mouthed in awe as an opera singer hits a soaring top note. Now, researchers at the University of Warwick have found that the indri, the world's only known singing lemur, appears to use a strikingly similar vocal technique to hit high notes.

items.title: Satellite record reveals Arctic melt season has plateaued after decades of lengthening
items.desc: For decades, Arctic sea ice has been melting earlier in spring and freezing later in fall, extending the melt season and contributing to widespread ice loss. A new NASA-led study published in Communications Earth & Environment has found that while the Arctic melt season has lengthened dramatically since satellite records began, that trend unexpectedly stabilized around 2010.

items.title: NASA just powered up Roman’s massive 300-megapixel camera
items.desc: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has successfully activated its 300-megapixel infrared camera, which will capture enormous stretches of the cosmos with Hubble-like sharpness. Its planet-hunting coronagraph is also working as expected, putting Roman another major step closer to beginning science operations in 2027.

items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
items.desc: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

items.title: A new process turns plastic waste into gasoline and diesel fuel
items.desc: Scientists at Oak Ridge National Laboratory have developed a surprisingly simple way to turn polyethylene, the common plastic used in shopping bags and cutting boards, into gasoline and diesel-like fuels. The process uses inexpensive aluminum-based molten salts to break long plastic molecules into smaller hydrocarbons, producing about 60% gasoline under relatively mild conditions.

items.title: Black holes of every size follow the same surprising rule
items.desc: Scientists have found evidence that black holes of vastly different sizes may launch powerful jets according to the same universal rule. Supermassive black holes can produce jets soon after tearing apart a star, then fire up again hundreds or thousands of days later when their feeding rate drops to about 2% of the Eddington limit. That same threshold is known to trigger jets from much smaller black holes in the Milky Way.

items.title: Chronic stress may be quietly reshaping your heart
items.desc: Chronic inflammation tied to stress, lifestyle, mental health, and socioeconomic conditions may silently change the heart for years before any symptoms appear. People with the highest inflammation levels faced a 43% greater risk of heart attack and stroke, raising hopes that earlier testing and anti-inflammatory treatments could help prevent serious heart disease.

items.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
items.desc: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

items.title: What kills Schrödinger’s cat? Gravity may not be the answer
items.desc: Physicists have put a decades-old idea about why the strange rules of quantum mechanics disappear in our everyday world to one of its toughest experimental tests yet. Deep beneath Italy’s Gran Sasso mountain, researchers searched for an extremely faint radiation signal predicted by a theory suggesting that tiny fluctuations in spacetime, caused by gravity, gradually destroy quantum superpositions. After 62 days of measurements with a highly shielded germanium detector, they found no such signal.

items.title: Scientists opened a sealed envelope after 10 years. Gravity still didn’t make sense
items.desc: A decade-long NIST experiment has produced a new measurement of the universal gravitational constant that differs unexpectedly from another leading result, deepening a 225-year-old physics puzzle. The discrepancy is tiny, but for one of nature’s most fundamental constants, it is large enough to keep scientists wondering whether hidden experimental errors or something more surprising is involved.

items.title: A giant crater may reveal the origin of Mars’ doomed moon
items.desc: A massive crater on Mars’ moon Phobos may hide a dense region of compressed material that could reveal whether the moon is a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact on Mars. Japan’s upcoming MMX sample return mission could provide the measurements and physical evidence needed to solve the mystery.

items.title: Hurricane Hunters reveal 4 warning signs that a storm is about to strengthen
items.desc: Nearly three decades of Hurricane Hunter data reveal four features that can help a tilted tropical cyclone straighten its circulation and become capable of intensifying. The findings could give forecasters an earlier warning that a seemingly disorganized storm is becoming primed to strengthen.

items.title: Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery
items.desc: Researchers may have solved a long-running mystery surrounding the Dead Sea Scrolls by proposing that the Qumran sect really did use its distinctive 364-day calendar. Its perfectly ordered 52-week system kept holidays on the same weekdays, but it slowly drifted out of sync with the seasons because it was shorter than the true solar year.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
items.desc: Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family.

items.title: New nanoparticles make hidden chemical differences light up
items.desc: Scientists have developed ultra-bright nanoparticles that can detect tiny amounts of chemicals and distinguish between molecules that look almost identical. The technology could one day provide a cheaper way to catch dangerous drug impurities or trace pollutants using simple low-cost lasers.

items.title: Ancient DNA reveals how plague kept returning for 400 years after the Black Death
items.desc: Ancient DNA reveals that plague repeatedly returned to Europe for more than 400 years after the Black Death, evolving into new lineages and spreading through trade, migration, and war. Researchers also developed a method to date ancient plague genomes more precisely, linking many of them to specific outbreaks recorded in historical sources.

items.title: Einstein’s “spooky action” just survived one of physics’ most extreme tests
items.desc: Physicists have detected strong evidence that heavy, fleeting Z bosons can become quantum entangled during Higgs boson decays at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. The result shows that Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” survives even under some of the most extreme conditions ever created in a laboratory.

items.title: A Central European Model for EU Growth
items.desc: As the European Union struggles to revive growth and loses ground to the United States and China, its economic future looks increasingly uncertain. Central Europe’s experience suggests that reversing that decline will require fostering innovation while helping poorer countries catch up.

items.title: Might Makes Right Will End Pax Americana
items.desc: Far from bolstering US dominance, Donald Trump’s embrace of coercive militarism has eroded it. When the distinction between war and peace dissolves into a ceasefire that is neither, and months of bombardment fail to deliver anything like victory, force looks less like strength and more like pointless destruction.

items.title: A Roadmap for the Next UN Secretary-General
items.desc: The next UN secretary-general will take over the most prominent position in multilateral governance at a time when multilateralism is arguably at its nadir. Adapting to today’s multipolar reality will require instilling a renewed sense of purpose and demanding more of member states.

items.title: A New World Order Is Not Beckoning
items.desc: It does no good to get misty-eyed about the demise of the liberal international “order.” What the world really needs to manage today's biggest risks is a different, more realistic narrative that does not draw a sharp line between a disintegrating ideal and its post-liberal successor.

items.title: What It Means for Global Warming to Exceed 1.5°C
items.desc: A sobering new report from the United Nations Environment Programme warns that even if governments deliver on all their existing climate pledges, warming could reach 1.8°C later this century. That means humanity must pivot from simply containing global warming to finding ways to reverse it.

The adaptation imperative may end up being the kind of crisis that forces us to stop neglecting the green agenda and act at the necessary scale.

items.title: Africa’s AI Opportunity
items.desc: The global AI revolution is often portrayed as a Sino-American race to develop the most advanced frontier models. But the greatest economic prize most likely will be found in deploying practical intelligence, particularly in Africa’s young, dynamic, and fast-growing economies.

items.title: The Political Earthquake From Germany’s China Shock
items.desc: For decades, Germany’s stability rested on an implicit bargain: high-value manufacturing would provide good jobs, strong export revenues, and broad-based prosperity, which political institutions would translate into social cohesion. Competition from China shakes that bargain to its foundations.

items.title: Stopping the Far Right’s Rise
items.desc: Leftists insist that what is behind the far right’s recent gains, from Europe to Central and South America, is economic precarity. Far-right leaders know better, winning elections or gaining support despite embracing very different economic policies.

items.title: A Congress for Europe’s Future
items.desc: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recently proposed Congress of Europe is a step in the right direction, given the scale of Europe's geopolitical challenges. But to succeed, it must address the shortcomings that have hampered similar efforts in the past.

items.title: Trump’s Iran Sanctions Have a China Problem
items.desc: US President Donald Trump is trying to pressure the Iranian regime by isolating it from the dollar-based financial system. But because Iran’s oil trade largely moves through Chinese banks and renminbi-based networks, those sanctions increasingly depend on financial institutions beyond American control.

items.title: When AI Stops Asking Permission
items.desc: The most useful lesson from this summer’s breach of Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI agents is about architecture, not intentions. AI agents need protective layers—limited access, separate authorization for sensitive actions, records nobody can quietly edit, and outside testing before deployment—not a lecture about good behavior.
